g.text: Three reservations per second - and the entire difficulty is one row
There is no throughput challenge here at all. This is correctness under contention, which is a different problem.
Two people looking at the last available room
user A
user B
room_type_inventory (hotel 245, king city view, 2026-06-01)
total_inventory 100
total_reserved 99 <- one room left
201 confirmed
409 no longer available
Both requests read the inventory, both see one room free, both write a
reservation - and now the hotel has sold a room it does not have. That is
a double-booking, and it is the kind of bug that produces a furious guest
standing in a lobby at 11pm. So the whole case study is about which of
these two requests wins, and how that decision is made atomically.
And note: losing the race is a
NORMAL outcome at peak season,
not an error. It must not be
logged as one or alerted on - a
lesson that recurs whenever a
design has a legitimate loser.
reserved + n <= total x 1.10
NOT reserved <= total. The hotel
deliberately WANTS to oversell:
cancellations are predictable in
aggregate, so selling 110% of
capacity means fuller hotels.
Which makes the invariant a business
rule that has to live somewhere
trustworthy - and that is a schema
question, not an application one.
The funnel - and what the numbers tell you to do
hotel page viewed
room-type detail viewed
reservation page viewed
~30/sec
reservation SUBMITTED
~3/sec
~1,000:1 read-to-write, and even the top of the funnel is only 3,000 requests/sec - trivially served by a cache and a read
replica, because hotel and room data is near-static and caches almost perfectly.
1,000,000 rooms x 70% occupancy / 3-day average stay
= ~233,000 reservations/day = ~2.7 per second
roughly 0.0008% of the digital wallet's peak
5,000 hotels x 20 room types x 365 days x 2-year
booking horizon = 73 MILLION rows
at ~50 bytes each = under 4 GB, one node,
indexes and all - pre-populated by a nightly cron
that extends the horizon by a day
So: DO NOT DISTRIBUTE THIS SYSTEM
One relational database with ACID transactions handles the entire
workload with orders of magnitude of headroom - and ACID is precisely
the tool the double-booking problem needs. The interesting engineering
is the choice among locking strategies, not sharding. (An interviewer
will pivot to 'now make it Booking.com': the answer is sharding by
hotel_id plus a CDC-fed cache - but reaching for it at 3 reservations/
sec would be building infrastructure for a problem that does not exist.)
Guests do not book a room. They book a room TYPE.
You reserve 'a king room with a city view' and the front desk assigns room 412 when you arrive. That is how hotels actually
work - and it differs from Airbnb (you book a specific listing) and from ticket booking (you book seat J14).
the unit of inventory is NOT a room:
it is a (hotel, room_type, date) triple carrying a COUNT
So the schema tracks HOW MANY of this type are taken on this date, rather than
WHICH rooms are occupied - and the concurrency control therefore protects a
COUNTER, not a row-level status flag.
a seat is a unique resource with a BINARY state
a room type is a numeric BUDGET
That difference is why this design's locking discussion looks nothing like the seat-booking one. Protecting a BUDGET admits
solutions that protecting a unique resource does not - an atomic conditional increment, a CHECK constraint - and the room-type
modelling decision is what makes them available.
One transaction does the hard part - and two things are deliberately kept out of it
BEGIN;
UPDATE room_type_inventory SET total_reserved = total_reserved + n
WHERE ... AND total_reserved + n <= total_inventory * 1.10;
COMMIT;
payment
it calls an external provider and can take SECONDS. A row lock held across a
third-party API call would serialize every booking for that hotel behind one
slow payment. So the reservation commits as pending, payment happens outside
the transaction, and a second transaction confirms it - the saga shape, for
the oldest reason there is: never hold a lock across a network call you do
not control.
a client-supplied reservation_id
generated when the user OPENS the booking form, acting as an idempotency key.
It is what makes a double-clicked Book button harmless - and it is a
completely different problem from two users racing.
Three API details that carry real weight
reservation_id is generated by the CLIENT, before submission
not by the server on receipt. The booking form generates a UUID when
it loads, so every submission of THAT FORM carries the same id: a
double-click, a refresh-and-resubmit and a flaky-network retry all
arrive identical, and the second is recognised as a replay.
Generating it server-side would defeat the whole mechanism, because
each retry would look like a fresh request.
availability returns a PER-NIGHT breakdown, not a boolean
a four-night stay can fail on exactly one night, and telling the user
'not available' without saying WHICH NIGHT is a bad product. It also
means the response carries the per-night rate, which the
daily-changing-prices requirement demands anyway.
409 is the expected outcome, not an error
at peak season, losing the race for the last room is a normal thing
that happens to real users. It must not be logged as an error or
alerted on.
